entries.note: From Greek [[from:komoidos]], a performer at festivals and revelries who put on komoidia, an amusing spectacle; a comedy need not be funny, but should be fun.
From Greek [[from:tragos]], goat, plus the -ody song ending shared with [[same-root:comedy]]: a goat song, perhaps because a goat was the prize in early ode competitions.
Satyr stories may explain the goat in [[see:tragedy]]; the Greek satyrs were long confused with [[unrelated:satire]], though the words have different origins.
A probably apocryphal tale says he won a goat as a prize in an acting competition, which may explain [[see:tragedy]]; namesake of [[gave:Thespians]].
Named after [[from:Thespis]], who supposedly won a goat in an acting competition.
A hymn sung to Dionysus, a predecessor of [[see:tragedy]], usually with a chorus of people dressed as [[see:satyr]]s.

From Latin [[from:satura]], a miscellany saturated with genres, related to [[same-root:saturate]], [[same-root:satisfy]] and [[same-root:satiate]]; its meaning shifted through confusion with the unrelated [[unrelated:satyr]].
Related to [[same-root:satire]] through Latin satura.
Related to [[same-root:satire]] through Latin satura.
Related to [[same-root:satire]] through Latin satura.
From French [[from:lampons]], let's drink, from a verb meaning to booze or guzzle; Jess recalls reading it may be related to [[same-root?:lap]].
Lap as in lapping up a drink, which Jess recalls reading may be related to [[same-root?:lampoon]].
Para, beside, as in [[same-root:parallel]], plus the -ody of [[same-root:tragedy]] and [[same-root:comedy]]; the first parodies were burlesque imitations of other genres.
Its para, meaning beside, is the same as in [[same-root:parody]].

Via 16th-century French from Italian [[from:burlesco]], ludicrous, from [[from:burla]]; first an English adjective meaning droll, later a variety show, with striptease added in late-19th-century America.
Italian for joke or mockery, also a comic interlude or practical joke inserted into a performance, often in [[see:commedia dell'arte]]; root of [[gave:burlesque]].
The suffix of [[see:burlesque]], meaning in the style of, which English tacks onto other words.
From Latin [[from:farcire]], to stuff, like French [[same-root:farci]]: first a silly interlude stuffed between serious plays, now comedy of escalating chaos and misunderstandings.
The French word for a dish with something stuffed inside, still the French word for stuffing, related to [[same-root:farce]].
An Italian device of two hinged pieces of wood that smack together, used in the wings or by clowns to make a hit sound far louder than it is.
Originally a clumsy country peasant, like [[see:villain]]; Germanic, probably meaning lump, perhaps related to [[same-root?:clue]]; the OED rejects a link with [[unrelated:colonist]].
Like [[see:clown]], it originally meant a person from the countryside or a peasant farmer, before taking on moral overtones.
A ball of thread, like the one leading through the Minotaur's labyrinth; its ball or lump sense may connect it with [[same-root?:clown]].
An older suggested source of [[unrelated:clown]], since it also meant farmer; the OED rejects it because the chronology doesn't fit.
Early professional Italian theatre, popular across Europe, with improvised formulaic scenes, masked stock characters and recurring routines; the source of many English comedy words.
A well-rehearsed joke or stock physical gag of [[see:commedia dell'arte]], plural lazzi, such as the [[see:lazzo of the mirror]].
A lazzo in which [[see:Pantalone]] and [[see:Il Dottore]] find a mirror whose reflections, other characters mimicking them, grow ever more absurd.
A lazzo in which [[see:Brighella]] cooks a meal, adding inedible ingredients like shoes and books while other characters taste it in horror.
A grumpy, elderly Venetian miser and merchant of commedia dell'arte with a high sex drive, whose distinctive red tights gave us [[gave:pantaloons]].
Named after [[from:Pantalone]] and his red tights; it later gave [[gave:pants]].
From [[from:pantaloons]], ultimately named after the commedia dell'arte character [[see:Pantalone]].
An arch servant character of commedia dell'arte, prone to playing tricks, whose name gave English [[gave:zany]].
From [[from:Zanni]]: someone was first called a zany, a tricky servant type, before the word came to mean a quirky character.
A Bergamese manservant of commedia dell'arte, invisible to [[see:Pantalone]] and so free for mischief; the name also covers his patterned costume and now suggests a jester.
A clever, manipulative and cruel masked servant of commedia dell'arte, star of the [[see:lazzo of the food]].
A servant character of commedia dell'arte who uses trickery and deception to help or hinder others.
A commedia dell'arte scholar or doctor who talks endlessly and presents himself as highly educated.
The soldier among the higher-class stock characters of commedia dell'arte.
From French [[from:disant]], one who speaks, spelling influenced by [[see:dizzy]]; first a court storyteller, then a fool and an insult; now lost.
Thought to have influenced the spelling of [[see:dizzard]].
Like [[see:dizzard]], it went from an entertaining fool to an insult, but unlike dizzard it survives.
From Italian via French [[from:bouffon]], perhaps onomatopoeic, its first syllable evoking puffing out your cheeks to get a laugh.
English rendering of French -on or Italian -one, as in [[see:lampoon]] and [[see:buffoon]]; spelled -oun in Middle English, found on pejorative words like [[see:shabbaroon]] and neutral ones.
A pejorative word with the [[see:-oon]] ending.
Another word with the [[see:-oon]] ending.
A word with the [[see:-oon]] ending that isn't pejorative.
Originally a story of achievements or adventures, like the [[see:Gesta Francorum]]; it later shrank to a less grand story told over ale; gave [[gave:jester]].
A famous medieval jest, a Latin chronicle of the First Crusade by the priest [[see:Fulcher of Chartres]], who took part in it.
From [[from:jest]]: originally a professional storyteller, minstrel or reciter of romances; by the 15th century any court entertainer, usually a silly one.
From Latin [[from:jocus]], with relatives such as French [[same-root:jeu]] and [[same-root:jouer]] and English [[same-root:jocular]] and [[same-root:jocund]].
A French relative of [[same-root:joke]].
A French relative of [[same-root:joke]].
Taken more directly from the Latin source of [[same-root:joke]].
Taken more directly from the Latin source of [[same-root:joke]].
A 20th-century term Jess linked to [[from?:Punch and Judy]]; Rob thinks it is more likely the closing line that gives a [[from?:punch]], delivering the impact.
A puppet show in a small booth where Punch and Judy beat each other with sticks, chased by a policeman; based on [[from:Pulcinella]].
A commedia dell'arte character, also involving a puppet, who gave rise to [[gave:Punch and Judy]].
A satirical magazine, known in America too, named after Punch, one of the two main characters of [[from:Punch and Judy]].
Not specifically a comedy word: it means to puncture or poke, from French [[from:poinçonner]], to punch, prick or stamp, and also names a pointed tool.
Originally a trick, not a joke; the OED suggests thrusting something down a credulous person's throat to see what they'll swallow, or it may imitate laughter.
A laughing word that may simply imitate a sound, as [[see:gag]] might.
A laughing word that may simply imitate a sound, as [[see:gag]] might.
A laughing word that may simply imitate a sound, as [[see:gag]] might.
A Scottish word, from a Scots verb [[from:gawf]], to laugh.
A portmanteau coined by [[see:Lewis Carroll]], perhaps of [[from?:chuckle]] and [[from?:snort]]; Britain has comedy awards called the [[see:Chortle Awards]].
British comedy awards, brought up while discussing [[see:chortle]].
Name for Tudor collections of humorous anecdotes, including [[see:A Hundred Merry Tales]], framed as influencing Shakespeare's humour; some jokes are absolutely filthy.
A 1526 joke collection compiled into [[see:Shakespeare's Jest Book]].
A 1530 joke collection compiled into [[see:Shakespeare's Jest Book]].
Referenced in [[see:Shakespeare's Jest Book]], they do ridiculous things to convince the king not to build his road through their town.
A tamer, mid-19th-century joke collection by [[see:Mark Lemon]], including a Quaker warning a man he might run his face against his fist.
British short form of [[from:pantomime]], which Jess hadn't heard before Rob mentioned it.
Originally a mime, a Roman performer acting myths through gesture; in Britain a Christmas fairy-tale play with music and cross-dressing, from [[from:commedia dell'arte]] via the [[see:Harlequinade]].
The [[see:pantomime]] stock character always played by a man, usually middle-aged, dressed as a woman and often the leading man's mother.
Call and response shouted back and forth with the audience at a [[see:pantomime]], answered by oh yes he did.
A line the audience shouts at a [[see:pantomime]].
A comic stage form based on commedia dell'arte figures, closely tied to British [[see:pantomime]], in which [[see:Harlequin]] gets a magic wand and drives chases and transformations.
Perhaps from French [[from?:chanson du vaudevire]], song of the Vire valley, linked with [[see:Olivier Basselin]], or from [[from?:vauder]] and [[from?:virer]]; -ville wrongly replaced -vire.
Rob's suggested British equivalent of [[see:vaudeville]], whose performers could sing, dance and do everything.
A 15th-century poet from Vire whose satirical popular songs may have given [[see:vaudeville]] its name.
Literally belly talking; it first described demonic possession with rumbling internal speech, then entertainers whose mouths you can't see moving.
From a trickery-based card game popularised in the 1880s by [[see:Arthur Roberts]]; like [[see:trumping]], spoofing meant tricking, then faking, as with radar, then a comic imitation.
A music hall comedian who invented or revived the card game that gave us [[gave:spoof]] in the 1880s.
From the game of trumps, a parallel to [[see:spoof]] coming from a card game.

From trans and [[from:vestire]], to clothe across, via [[from:travestir]], dressed in disguise; first a burlesque keeping a serious work's characters, then any grotesque distortion; a doublet of [[same-root:transvestite]].
One of the earliest phrases using [[see:travesty]] for a grotesquely inadequate version of something.
Etymologically means the same as [[same-root:travesty]], which is a figurative wearing of someone else's clothes.
Another word using the idea of clothing figuratively, like [[see:travesty]].
Basically a doublet of [[same-root:travesty]], with a different ending and sense.
An early-20th-century New York publisher of cheap paperbound joke books, parlour tricks, magic and songbooks, which collected family-friendly vaudeville jokes.
Its origin is unclear; Rob says it's just a syllable, with little to go on.
